Looking at EM bond inflows in a similar way, we also see the same pattern. Historically, foreign ownership data in EM bonds has increased over time, but “T” regimes have shown the lowest inflows. In particular, high-yielding bond markets have even seen outflows when US real rates sell off and inflation breakevens decline (Figure 4). Counterintuitively, a BERT Recession (“R”) regime (real rates and inflation breakevens both fall) seems to be the best for bond inflows. However, this likely reflects fixed income inflows kicking off after the initial risk sell-off and a greater tilt toward low-yielders in EM rather than the higher-yielding/high-beta complex. More tactical approach needed against cyclical headwinds: As even an aggressive Fed looks unlikely to derail risk assets completely, we think the market will mostly fluctuate between BERT’s “T” and Expansion (“E”) regimes. These periods of volatility could be used to add to EM longs, either via FX carry trades or for some secular duration exposures where valuations are attractive. Differences in domestic fundamentals and central bank reaction functions are likely to drive relative performance, with a lower volatility regime likely in most markets. Hawkish Fed communication and resilient US growth should sustain a wider n distribution around the US front-end and present an obstacle to meaningful US outperformance versus other markets. Fundamental weakness and elevated hike premium leave the UK front-end the clearest long. The belly of US and European curves should outperform, whereas we see a n clearer case for steepening the UK curve given the overhang of macro and fiscal risk premia. Limited room for materially lower yields leaves carry an important part of rates n portfolios. We expect the RBA will remain on hold at 4.35% through mid-2027 as they balance above-target inflation against downside growth/labour risks. New Zealand’s economy is forecast to grow by 1.5% in 2026 despite a contraction in mid-2026, while the RBNZ gradually tightens to address above-target inflation of 3.4% in 2026. Australia: RBA balancing conflicting objectives Australian growth has been revised down to 1.8% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027 (from 2.0% and 2.3%), reflecting a hawkish RBA pivot leading to a more restrictive stance, higher inflation and softer growth momentum due to the global energy shock (Exhibit 30). Growth had already begun to moderate ahead of the energy shock and is likely to slow further in mid-2026 as higher energy prices, weaker real incomes, and elevated uncertainty weigh on consumption and investment. The fiscal impulse is also slightly weaker than expected, contributing to growth remaining below trend in 2026 and 2027 as private demand faces ongoing headwinds despite a still-tight labour market (see Budget review report). Since the conflict began, energy-sensitive CEE and Asian markets in particular have started to show much stronger correlations between their currencies and rates. This is intuitive as the energy price shock was both a balance of payments problem that weakened currencies and an inflation problem that pushed rates higher (Figure 5). However, for the rest of EM (usually the more risk- sensitive high-beta complex), FX-rates correlations remain relatively similar to levels in developed markets (Figure 6). Therefore, a normalisation in energy markets should once again lower these correlations for the asset class and help to sustain inflows, in our view. Rates-induced sell-off most risky for EM: In terms of total returns from local currency bonds in EM, this year the asset class’s correlations with US equities and US rates have risen significantly. This means a rates-induced sell-off in risk assets could be the most damaging outcome for EM local bond portfolios (Figure 7). Silver lining: Despite the increased correlation of EM local bonds to US rates and equities, EM FX carry remains more secular. In particular, EM high-beta funded out of equity-sensitive, low-yielding Asia mitigates some of the asset class’s increased beta (Figure 7). However, if the productivity boost is in the non - tradeble sector, the opposite happens. Competition is driven by domestic firms, meaning that with a productivity boom these firms will reduce prices to attract more customers, which lowers the overall price level, contributing to lower yields and thus a weaker currency. These firms tend to not increase wages. But if they were to do so then that would prove negative for the tradeable sector since they must match that without an associated productivity boost, thus reducing margins. In this instance, a productivity boost would actually be FX negative. AI disproportionately improves productivity in non - tradeable sectors Our expectation is that AI will disproportionately boost productivity in non - tradeable sectors, i.e. services. That’s not to say that tradable sectors will not benefit. After all, the US is already a large producer of many high value exports. However, more fragmented global trade policy and tariffs may play a role in diminishing that boost. Data tends to support this. Historically, EM local currency bonds and EM FX carry did not perform very well when US rates are rising. Firstly, higher rate differentials support the US dollar and secondly tightening financial conditions weigh on risk assets and trigger a flight to safety leading to outflows from EM assets. This time around we expect the USD strength to be milder than historical patterns despite the Fed hikes and we have revised our FX forecasts implying a flat USD TWI until year- end. The diversification of global portfolios away from the US dollar and resulting structural flows partially offset the cyclical tailwind for the greenback from higher rates and limit the extent of the FX impact on EM. We also think that 75bp of tightening does not shift the US policy to an excessively restrictive stance especially given the starting point of elevated inflation, robust earnings growth, loose fiscal and tight labour markets. So, we do not expect these hikes to derail the global risk backdrop completely even if the path could be bumpier with bouts of volatility. So, we think the EM local currency bond returns will remain somewhat in a positive territory for the rest of the year. We had expected the MPC to be proactive to counter the possibility of second round effects, given above- target inflation in past few years, high inflation expectations and UK’s past susceptibility to inflation persistence. But it appears to us that the BoE would only act if the energy shock is prolonged or clear, strong evidence emerges on signs of second round effects, risks of which it judges is higher the longer high energy prices persist. The BoE looks to be taking comfort from tightening in financial conditions and the Bank Rate being restrictive. This suggests the MPC is willing to tolerate above target inflation temporarily, as long as second round effects are contained. records.text: dle East conflict escalated, but we have yet to see any evidence of spending being cut back. GDP data shows private consumption grew a decent 0.3% q/q in Q1 2026. Retail sales climbed 1.3% m/m in April (they were also 1.3% higher than the Q1 average). Similarly, the Bank of Japan's consumption activity index was up 1.6% m/m in April (and 1.3% from Q1). Some allowance does need to be made for the impact of changes to the tax system on automobile sales in April, but it seems clear to us that the gradual recovery in household spending has yet to be derailed. We think steady growth in nominal wages and government energy subsidies likely contributed to the resilience in consumption. In addition, recent spending may have been buoyed to some degree by a sustained rise in stock prices driven by the AI boom. Growing popularity of the Nippon Individual Savings Account scheme has seen many households increase allocation to risk assets, thereby creating potential for the wealth effect to have more of an impact on private consumption than in the past. The BoJ's Flow of Funds data shows that the percentage of household financial assets held as equities or investment trusts has risen from an average of 13% in the 2010s to 22% as at Q4 2025. This share could have expanded further on the back of the stock market's subsequent stellar gains. Capex appetite still elevated: Domestic firms appear to remain keen on capital investment as they continue to enjoy solid demand, both at home and abroad.

records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 25 June 2026 41 Colombia: Preparing to take the fiscal medicine Elephant in the room in Colombia is fiscal Fiscal adjustment in Colombia is unavoidable. The de la Espriella administration, to assume office on 7 August – will inherit a fiscal deficit above 7% of GDP and rising public debt. 10-year local currency government bond yields surpassed 14% in May, before the first round of the presidential elections, causing the impression that borrowing costs were spiraling out of control. Nevertheless, after the election of Abelardo de la Espriella as the new president of Colombia (for the term 2026-2030), markets gave the government a respite. The 10-year yield dropped below 12%. The reason is that de la Espriella is proposing a large fiscal adjustment, which we think is critical to regain the confidence of markets. We forecast a fiscal consolidation of 1.5pp of GDP in the primary balance for 2027, and 1pp for 2028. After that, the consolidation would be more gradual, reaching at least 3 percentage points of GDP, cumulatively, during the first three years. Central Bank (BanRep) may reward the government with cuts next year Central bankers in Colombia blame fiscal slippage as one of the reasons for why inflation has been above the tolerance range for six consecutive years. In principle, this should have freed up additional capacity to absorb new demand. On the supply side, labour shortages and bureaucratic constraints may help explain why the backlog remained broadly unchanged. On the demand side, some projects may still be in the pipeline, with developers waiting for a more supportive investment environment. Interestingly, construction backlogs vary substantially across the German states. Brandenburg, Berlin, and Bavaria have particularly high ratios—at around 2.5% relative to the total housing stock. These regions are home to strong economic centres, including Berlin/Potsdam and Munich. By contrast, the only states with comparatively low backlogs, close to the natural level (below 1%), are Saarland, Saxony-Anhalt, and Thuringia. These states share several common characteristics: they are small, lack a major urban centre, and, above all, have shrinking populations. As a result, weak demand appears to matter more than a more elastic supply side due to an efficient bureaucracy and many workers. Equity inflows are through financial centers and are more actively managed, making the US financial account structurally vulnerable Portfolio inflows into US equities are dominated by two key regions: the eurozone and the Caribbean (Figure 10). Within the EU, the largest inflow is not from the likes of Germany but rather via Ireland, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. In other words, US equity inflows reflect demand from financial centers (Figure 11). The investor types operating through these regions are unclear, i.e. whether they are retail (similar to Asia), fast money, or re-routing by European real money for tax purposes. Regardless, this indicates that investors now are more actively managing their equity exposure in search of returns. Structurally, we think this makes the US financial account more vulnerable. If investors are now accumulating US equities more actively than passively, they will similarly be more willing to sell these stocks on any signs of weakness, which can translate into significant USD outflows. In other words, their holdings are now considerably less sticky than before. We had expected Warsh’s refusal to provide either a “dot” or verbal guidance about upcoming rate decisions but his broader comments on Fed communications with financial markets went further: “So I think financial markets perform best when they react to incoming data. I think the financial markets work less efficiently when they ask [the] question ‘how will the Federal Reserve react to that incoming information?’ The more that markets are paying attention to what’s happening in the real economy, deciding what’s good data and what’s less good data, the more financial markets can price what they believe is the most likely and what are the tail risks.” Since the Fed essentially controls short-term interest rates and the interest rate path matters for asset pricing, it is inevitable that markets ask how the Fed will react to incoming information. Admittedly, this can turn into an unproductive obsession with computing the Fed’s reaction function, which is often harder to summarize and subject to greater change than many market participants think. Still, a significant reduction in Fed transparency could make financial conditions—and thus economic outcomes— more volatile as market assumptions about the Fed’s thinking become subject to fewer reality checks. Evidently, the AI investment boom is an engine of global growth at the moment, as showcased by booming exports in China and the rest of EM Asia. Concerns about overcapacity, most notably in Europe, are unlikely to dissipate any time soon in this context. Inflation is a worsening problem in the US For a long time, we have been clear that the US economy was not asking for rate cuts, and our prospects for any monetary easing were largely based on the changes in Fed leadership. However, the outlook is shaping up with a stronger labor market and higher inflation that is not just driven by the energy shock. A shifting balance of risks The new reality of a stronger labor market with a recovery in payrolls and low and stable unemployment rate reduces the need for monetary policy to guard against downside risks. Importantly, additional upside risks from shocks such as El Niño and the 6x1 work shift change point to greater inflation persistence ahead, increasing inertia and complicating the policy trade-off. In this environment, the room for further easing is limited, and the bar for additional cuts has become meaningfully higher, consistent with a return to a “higher-for-longer” backdrop. That said, we do not see rate hikes on the horizon. As inflation embarks on a convergence trajectory, but fiscal uncertainty looms, we expect four consecutive 25bp cuts in 1H28, followed by a pause until year-end. This would leave the Selic at 12.25% by YE28. The recent deterioration in the inflation outlook, which motivated our policy rate review, reflects both external factors (prolonged war and El Niño) and internal ones (activity stimulus measures). We continue to expect inflation of 5.5% for YE26; however, we are raising our YE27 forecast to 4.7% (from 4.0%) to incorporate the inflationary effects of these events. Thereafter, we expect one additional hike to 1.75% by Oct ’27, pushed back from July previously. The delay reflects several factors. Second, the dovish dissent by Takaichi appointee Asada Toichiro at the Jun MPM suggests that hikes, especially beyond 1.5%, could expose greater disagreement on the Policy Board, particularly in light of further composition changes over the next year. Third, our strategists’ updated forecasts point to lower oil prices and a modestly stronger yen. The timing and pace of hikes could shift, with a weaker yen the most likely catalyst for a more front‑loaded path. But uncertainty around the timing of further hikes and the terminal rate remains significant. records.text: Ning Sun 25 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Emerging Markets Weekly: Limited Upside for USD Strength Last week's EMFX rally was interrupted by the hawkish FOMC outcome and the subsequent rebound in the USD, despite renewed progress in the Middle East conflict and the associated decline in oil prices. Our flow data continued to show outflows from both EM equity and fixed -income asset classes, highlighting a still-cautious investor backdrop. While EMFX registered a modest five -day inflow, we believe this reflects FX hedge unwinds accompanying broader portfolio reductions. Looking ahead, we expect the latest bout of USD strength to have a more limited impact on EM currencies than on their developed -market counterparts. In our view, the Fed is largely playing catch-up to the EM central bank hawkishness . At the same time, lower oil prices are improving external balances across much of the EM universe, reducing external vulnerabilities and allowing policymakers to focus more on domestic growth considerations. As a result, we remain relatively constructive on EMFX even during periods of renewed USD strength. With a full resolution yet to be finalized with regard to the Strait of Hormuz, and resumption of oil flows expected at a gradual pace, the path of oil and read- throughs for inflation and growth remains the key swing factor over the next several weeks. The duration of the energy disruption is consequential — our base case assumes crude back to $90/bbl at the end of the year and further declines in 2027, close to our oil strategists' most recent update on the oil price path. A more protracted oil price dislocation would exacerbate growth and inflation risks, and a permanent risk premium for oil would stall the return to target inflation globally. Ex-energy price volatility, global growth is fundamentally supported by continued US momentum in AI-driven capex and consumer spending. While real consumption growth is expected to be soft in coming quarters as energy prices weigh on disposable income, underlying consumption trends remain robust with a more stable labor market. There is a bit of irony that market pricing remains hostage to Fed guidance at a time when Warsh is openly expressing his disdain for forecasts. This contempt manifested itself in one less projection and one less dot as Warsh withheld his view on the path for Fed Funds and the economy. The +38 bps shift in the 2026 dots nonetheless has opened the door for investors to openly consider hikes in the near term, with nearly 50 bps of tightening now priced in through mid-2027. To be sure, this is more aggressive than the dots, which has the one hike this year reversing itself in 2027. Additionally, only 1 or 2 votes separate each of these views, hardly a sign of unified plurality Of course, a hike that is reversed in quick succession is not how monetary policy functions, so investors will be free to continue their hawkish lean until data proves otherwise. We therefore are hesitant to fade the rates move, as we think there is a strong growth component to this tightening bias, with economic activity and labour strength a continued tailwind for U.S. investors. records.text: since late last year and up 64.1% y/y as at April on the back of particularly strong demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Further, more timely machine-tool orders data indicates foreign demand remained strong even as at May. The AI boom also appears to be boosting demand for a wide range of other capital goods from Japan, including air-conditioning systems for data centres as well as fibre- optic cables. Overall export volume has stalled of late due to a dramatic downturn in shipments to the Middle East, but we expect the latter to rebound if and when the Strait of Hormuz is fully reopened, and the aforementioned strength of capital goods orders in any case appears conducive to exports staging a recovery. Export prices rising: The positive impact of the AI investment boom is evident not only in volume but also in pricing. Export prices have risen markedly since H2 2025 – thereby providing a significant boost for corporate earnings – not just for the semiconductor industry but also for other sectors such as non-ferrous metals. The overall export price index rose 11.7% y/y in May even on a contract-currency basis, with electric and electronic products recording a sharper 23.9% increase. The AI boom has also been driving up prices for imported raw materials, but has ultimately constituted a positive shock to the terms of trade as Japan plays a key role in relevant supply chains. We do not expect the BCCh to resume tightening while markets continue to underprice the risk of higher rates should inflation prove more persistent. As a result, the central bank is likely to remain on hold for an extended period while assessing the extent of second-round inflation effects. In Colombia, higher energy prices provide support to the external sector and activity, but they also reinforce an already difficult inflation backdrop. BanRep surprised markets by holding rates at 11.25% in April despite expectations for a hike. Sticky inflation, de- anchored expectations and resilient domestic demand continue to argue for additional tightening, and we expect a further 250bp of hikes, taking the policy rate to 13.75%. Beyond the macro outlook, political and institutional developments remain important drivers of risk, including the presidential election and ongoing questions surrounding the independence of monetary policymaking. In Peru, macroeconomic conditions remain among the strongest in the region, supported by a broad recovery in domestic demand and improving confidence. While headline inflation remains elevated due to transport and supply-related pressures, underlying inflation measures remain considerably more benign. records.text: 06/2026 Path from LGE 2026 to ANC 2027 conference How an ANC elective conference works: The national conference is the ANC's highest decision-making body and meets every five years, with the branch as its ‘basic units’. After the November 2026 local elections, branches in good standing will hold branch general meetings to nominate candidates and elect delegates, who make up roughly 90% of the voting floor; the rest are drawn from the provinces and the Youth, Women's and Veterans' Leagues. Delegations are split equally by gender. By secret ballot, and on a simple majority, the conference elects the 'Top Seven' officials and the wider National Executive Committee. The 2007 conference in Polokwane 2007, where Jacob Zuma unseated Thabo Mbeki as party leader, is the precedent for an incumbent being overturned. The integrity of these branch processes – in particular, membership in good standing and the credentialing of delegates – is routinely contested, and the party itself has conceded that disputes of this kind can cloud the legitimacy of an outcome.

GOVERNANCE INSTABILITY AND SYSTEMIC WEAKNESS How local incumbents have survived – until now: Despite steadily deteriorating service quality, three mechanisms have protected the ANC in local government, in our view. ▪ Patronage dependency: When the governing coalition in a local government controls resource distribution even when it has failed on service delivery, continued support is rational for vulnerable households. ▪ Political identity: The ANC's liberation legacy had previously created an accountability asymmetry, whereby voters ‘punish’ individual ANC ward councillors while continuing to vote for the party in the proportional representation vote. ▪ Disengagement: Turnout fell to a record-low 46% in the LGE 2021. With 35% of a shrinking pool, a party can govern with fewer absolute votes than before. As all three of the above mechanisms have continued to weaken simultaneously, several smaller parties have threatened ANC administrative control in key metros, shifting the patronage calculation for grant-dependent voters. For example, the historical legitimacy premium is generationally declining — 2026 first-time voters were born in 2007–08, long after the first democratic elections in 1994. We close the trade idea we initiated in FX: Adding a tactical AUDNZD long on 15 June for a profit of 0.72% (USD36k, spot ref: 1.22 22). The initial rationale for the trade was to position ahead of the Reserve Bank of Australia meeting and Q1 GDP report in New Zealand. The two events posed risks for front -end rates in opposite directions, which would have put upward pressure on the cross. The outlook at the RBA meeting was more balanced and Q1 GDP in New Zealand came in stronger than anticipated. We find it encouraging that despite neither catalyst materialising in a direction that would be supportive , the cross still trended higher , highlighting that our position was the correct one to capture the event asymmetry. We held the position through Australia’s May CPI report for a similar rationale but now opt to move to the sidelines ahead of the country’s May employment report. Upping our growth forecasts: We raise our Japan GDP growth forecast to 0.8% for CY2026 (from 0.5%) and 1.1% for CY2027 (from 0.7%) to reflect not only apparent improvements in the Middle East situation but also the broadening benefits of the AI-related investment boom. We have also made explicit allowance for the government's (seemingly almost finalised) plan to cut the consumption tax on food from 8% to 1% for two years starting April 2027. There is still a risk that Middle East tensions could flare up again. However, with the Japanese economy having so far held up better than we had originally envisaged, our overall assessment is that there is now an increasing likelihood of performance remaining solid beyond the middle of this year. Even after the revision, we believe that the balance of risks remains skewed to the upside, with domestic demand set to receive a further boost from expansionary fiscal policy settings in 2027. Strength in manufacturing indicators: Manufacturing indicators have been generally solid of late. Industrial production defied market expectations by increasing in April, with the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry forecast survey suggesting a further rise in May and June production

records.text: 10 Local government mandate on the ballot: The SRF/The Common Sense poll (March 2026) confirms that the issues South Africans consider most pressing combine national, provincial and municipal deliverables. Jobs and unemployment, the top priority for voters in the survey, are generally but not exclusively seen as the purview of national and provincial rather than municipal government. Of the other top concerns, water, roads, housing and electricity are the ones where municipalities are the primary delivery authority. Their combined weight among cited concerns is not a coincidence, in our view, but reflects the accumulated cost of two decades of municipal decay, which is now becoming more evident in failing levels of basic service delivery in even the largest metropolitan municipalities in core economic hubs of the country, namely Gauteng. General focus on practical delivery: The signature issues of the most vocal opposition parties, the EFF and MK, ranked at the bottom of the survey: racism and land reform. This suggests an electorate preferring service delivery rather than redistributive politics. However, illegal immigration ranked second in the poll with 23.3% – a level we have not seen in any comparable South African poll of the past decade. This concern appears to be concentrated in Gauteng and Cape Town metros, closely associated with Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA politics. records.Author: Marvin Loh
records.text: Marvin Loh 24 June 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : Warsh strait talk KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Under new management. The FOMC meeting proved to be a tradeable event even if Chairman Warsh went to great lengths to discredit the use of forward guidance, in living his principles, he abstained from providing his economic and rates views in the SEP, which left the door open for the remaining members to signal a rate hike this year. There continues to be a thin majority, with one vote separating the median from doing nothing this year. Directionally, we are still more hawkish from March’s projections, which has been supported by inflation remaining above target, while jobs and the economy have proven surprisingly resilient. This has allowed the FOMC to focus more on price stability, with Warsh signalling that regaining control of inflation remains job #1. This was well received by rate investors, who flattened the curve with the 2y repricing upwards of 18bps higher, while the 10y yields were less than ½ that amount. And while bear flattening can be viewed as a recessionary signal, we think that growth is a large part of this trade, which ultimately is a positive economic development. This growth impulse will partially offset gains in inflation on the reopening of the strait, with the potential that the strong retail sales figure during the middle of the conflict (which corresponded with high gas prices) has room to run further.

Early signs of sentiment deterioration. Our credit specialists highlight a notable shift in investor sentiment toward AI's impact on IG credit quality in The High- Grade Beat: Everyone’s an AI Adopter. From Figure 25, we show that nearly half of investors surveyed expected a net positive credit impact from generative AI in August last year. However, by June 2026, that view has completely flipped, with 47% now expecting credit degradation. This souring is driven by two forces: 1) the unprecedented scale of AI-related debt issuance that is mainly driven by Hyperscalers and 2) growing concerns that AI disruption could erode the business models of incumbent issuers. Our analysis indicates that the breakeven yield for bond ETF investors – using the 30y UST as a benchmark – is around 3.4-3.5%, significantly below the current 5% level. Hence, if the market assigns a larger fiscal premium to the US long end, we may see liquidation of bond ETFs by Taiwanese retail investors (who are more sensitive to market volatility), especially when TWSE equities continue to benefit from global optimism on AI. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 25 June 2026 3 From trade war to Iran war to Fed War-sh… Since February, the rollercoaster of Trump policies shifted focus from the trade war to the more disruptive Iran war, with the persistent narrative of a deal always approaching. Now, the temporary deal has apparently brought relief for at least 60 days, and this fragile peace could be extended even if fundamental agreement is not reached. In this context, our Commodities team has lowered their oil price forecasts to average $72/bbl in 2H 2026, and around $65/bbl in 2027, from $88/bbl and $72/bbl, respectively. But risks remain. In turn, the labor market firmed up and inflation dynamics have deteriorated in the US, as core services picked up, core goods kept rising, and housing disinflation has mostly run its course. While some one-offs are partly to blame, and tariffs should soon roll off, most of the FOMC seems to be losing patience after 5 years of high inflation and more recurrent supply shocks. We have been clear since the beginning of the year that despite the decoupling between consumption and the labor market, the US economy was not asking for cuts, but we now expect 75bp of Fed hikes this year, starting in September. The hawkish tone of the new Fed Chair, combined with an emerging consensus within the FOMC on the need to tighten policy, lead us to think that this is now the path of least resistance despite some important upcoming changes in the communication strategy of the Fed. The Ramaphosa question: The assumption that Ramaphosa is a stable anchor through 2029 now carries genuine uncertainty. A Constitutional Court ruling last month has revived a potential impeachment process against him (see, for example, BBC News, 8 May). The president is now seeking both to set aside the underlying panel report that found prima facie evidence that he had violated the constitution and to stay the impeachment inquiry by a parliamentary committee. The review application to the High Court against the panel report could run for up to a year; meanwhile, the work of the committee might ultimately recommend a parliamentary impeachment vote, in which case impeachment would require a two-thirds majority of National Assembly members. The matter is likely to shadow Ramaphosa into the pre-conference period. How the DA handles any vote would itself be a test of the GNU coalition. An additional consideration is that the impeachment process would be overseen by the Speaker, Thoko Didiza, herself mooted as a successor to Ramaphosa. Decline in price dispersion Asquith, Covert and Pathak (2013) show that the introduction of TRACE reduced price dispersion in the US corporate bond market. Prior to TRACE, two investors buying the same bond on the same day could receive materially different prices, largely because neither had visibility into recent transactions. Following the introduction of transparency, dispersion declined by 20-25% as valuation uncertainty fell and both dealers and investors converged around a tighter range of fair values. 7. More delayed spots and agency trades In the US, over 15% of volumes executed in US IG corporate bonds are delayed spot trades (Figure 9). These trades are negotiated during the day on a spread-to-Treasury basis, but the final pricing – or 'spotting' – is deferred until later, typically at 4:00pm, using that day's closing Treasury yields. Because TRACE requires trades to be reported only once full pricing information is known, these transactions are disseminated after the relevant Treasury levels are set, rather than at the point of initial agreement. As transparency increases in Europe with the introduction of consolidated tapes, similar mechanisms could become more prevalent. External story is strong but might cool with oil prices Nigeria’s external position remains one of the more constructive parts of the macro story. Current account surpluses, stronger inflows and a more orderly Fx market are supporting reserve accumulation, with gross reserves now approaching US$50bn and still offering scope to rise further over time. That said, if oil prices normalise with a more stable Hormuz, the pace of reserve build-up could slow, and the Naira may remain broadly range-bound around current spot levels rather than continue to strengthen materially. Even so, the broader picture remains supportive, with improved Fx liquidity and more credible two-way price action helping rebuild confidence. Fiscal noise still clouds an otherwise improving story Fiscal policy remains the main inconsistency in an otherwise improving macro mix. A statistical discrepancy of around 2.7% of GDP in 2025 points to spending outside the budget and suggests the true fiscal impulse may be less benign than headline numbers imply. Still, the direction of travel over the medium-term is clearer. Stronger revenue mobilisation, slower capex growth and better-targeted social transfers could help shift the stance from expansionary to more neutral. Taiwan’s central bank, the CBC, notes that the range which permits the TWD to have “dynamic stability” is if the TWD NEER is within ±5% of its three-year moving average (Figure 10 , CBC, Chinese only). And we think the range will be kept well this year. The CBC’s sufficient FX reserves and the trust it has built with market participants have helped keep USDTWD in a 27-35 range for the past 30 years. It is also why the TWD is more stable than the JPY and KRW, in our view. Earlier this year, local news suggested that the CBC was encouraging exporters to offer more USD while oil prices were high (MoneyUDN, dated 30 April, Chinese only); essentially the authorities are utilising flexible policy tools to curb imported inflation, in our view. We believe the authorities’ bias towards a strong TWD has waned, alongside fading concerns about oil-price- driven inflation and inflation expectations. Going forward, we think the Taiwanese authorities are still committed to keeping USDTWD stable, balancing regional beta (CNH, JPY, KRW) and will make the TWD a medium-range performer among six major currencies it stated on daily FX update - EUR, JPY, KRW, CNH, SGD

We believe this is the early stage of a bottoming process that can extend further as we move through the 2nd half of the year. The Consumer space bore the brunt of the geopolitical shock, facing the headwinds of elevated oil prices, sharply higher bond yields, and confidence readings that collapsed to multi- year lows. records.text: 2 Global Economic Viewpoint | 25 June 2026 Global letter: Hydration Break Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS Mid-Year review: Fragile peace meets a hawkish Fed The global economy continues to show strong signs of resilience. The peace deal, although fragile in nature, induced a new round of changes in our energy and macro forecasts, partially reversing the stagflationary shock of the war. But the underlying structural themes highlighted in our Year Ahead reports are still the order of the day: Trump policies, the AI boom, China’s overcapacity, fiscal imbalances, and excess global liquidity. The AI boom, fiscal imbalances, and easy financial conditions have supported K-shaped dynamics for the US and global economy through wealth effects, but this same pillar of resilience could turn into a source of weakness if there is a significant correction in asset prices. We mark up global growth to 3.2% for this year and expect it to accelerate to 3.5% in 2027. We mark down global headline inflation to 3% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027. But persistent inflation leads us to expect 75bp of Fed hikes and the ECB to deliver one more hike. In other words, the damage is already done, and even if we go back to pre- war levels of energy prices, we are not going to fully reverse the stagflationary shock. records.text: Ning Sun Noel Dixon 22 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General USMCA Review: How investors should trade around this risk ? While investors remain focused on the elusive Iran-US ceasefire, they may be overlooking another potential tail risk: the USMCA review scheduled for 1 July. The stakes are high, especially after US President Trump recently said, “I’m not looking to renew i t.” If the agreement were dissolved, the economic fallout for Canada, Mexico and the US could be substantial. This piece assesses the likelihood of a USMCA withdrawal or major revisions. Although the process could take months to conclude, we expect headlin e risk to emerge early in the negotiations. We therefore outline how investors may want to position ahead of this risk. USMCA RISK UNDERPRICED? While investors remain focused on the Iran -US Memorandum of Understanding, they appear to be overlooking another potential tail risk: the USMCA review scheduled for 1 July. That lack of focus looks striking given the scale of the economic exposure. Annual trade among the three countries totals about $1.8tn, equivalent to roughly 60% of Mexico’s GDP, 50% of Canada’s GDP and 10% of US GDP. On this theme, for much of the post-war period, UK politics offered investors something close to institutional predictability. Prime ministers came and went, but the rhythm was familiar: a general election, a mandate, several years of policy execution, and then either renewal or defeat. Over the last decade, that pattern has broken down. Since David Cameron resigned after the Brexit referendum in 2016, the UK has moved through Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak and now Keir Starmer in unusually rapid succession. The obvious explanation is Brexit, but the deeper point is that Brexit exposed structural weaknesses that the UK, like many other Western economies, face. First, the UK has become harder to govern. Brexit reordered party coalitions, regional voting patterns and policy priorities. It created a permanent tension between economic pragmatism and political symbolism, particularly on trade, migration, regulation and the role of the state. Prime ministers have repeatedly found that winning the leadership is easier than constructing a durable governing settlement and policies to deal with these tensions. Second, fiscal room has narrowed. The 2010s were defined by austerity; the 2020s by pandemic debt, energy shocks, higher rates and weaker productivity. Local banks are already holding a large inventory of bonds on their balance sheets, and with increasing credit growth, they may not be able to absorb the increased bond supply. This will steepen the bond curve further in our opinion. Fiscal ceiling may be increased: As we look ahead to 2027, Thailand's debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to continue its upward trend, gradually approaching the debt ceiling of 70%. While this may remain a potential concern for investors, we believe that Thailand may be able to increase its fiscal ceiling without triggering an adverse market reaction if it can sustain its current economic growth momentum. In any case, we expect the yield curve to steepen further, driven by either increased fiscal spending and bond issuances, or a larger term premium. Curve can steepen further: Although the yield curve has already steepened significantly since late 2025, we believe that it can continue to do so. For comparison, the 1s5s curve previously steepened to 70-80bp levels in 2016-2018 (Figure x), when the BoT kept interest rates on hold at 1.5% and the market did not expect any rate hikes. Given the current supportive factors, including increased fiscal spending, bond supply dynamics, improving economic momentum, and an anchored BoT policy stance, we think that the curve can continue to steepen from its current level. records.text: d rates came down as policy rate hike expectations were trimmed, and equities rallied. The Fed meeting was interpreted as a hawkish shift, implying higher short rates, a flatter curve, and equities softened some. We have to take the events together, though. Lower oil prices, if sustained, remove a lot of inflationary pressures in many economies. Greater chances of Fed hikes, however, means that other central banks may have to be more defensive. Previously, we have emphasized that a Fed hiking cycle driven by strong growth would have important global implications, particularly through financial conditions and the dollar. That narrative remains relevant, but the current environment adds an important layer. How much with the shift from the Fed sustain if inflation really does come down as we expect? Our baseline view remains that the Fed will stay on hold this year, and we see the recent market repricing after Chairman Warsh’s first FOMC meeting as somewhat overdone. In particular, the median Fed forecast was for 3.3% core PCE inflation this year, well above our call for 3%. Tariff-related inflation is fading, and much lower oil prices mean “second-round effects” are unlikely. So the median FOMC participant who is looking to hike once this year but cut next year, would need to reconsider if inflation proves notably more tame than expected. records.text: Racing for AI in a different way On the surface, China’s AI capex appears to fall far short of that in the US. For example, while US hyperscalers Amazon, Meta, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle are estimated to increase capex to over $750bn in 2026, Chinese hyperscalers Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, and Baidu are expected to reach only $100bn in total capex this year (Exhibit 7). However, this does not mean China’s computing power is only a fraction of that in the US. As of mid-2025, installed data center capacity in China was already 60% of that in the US (Exhibit 8). Two factors contributed to China’s low hyperscaler capex relative to its data center capacity. First, the cost of building data centers is much lower in China than in the US. Second, a significant share of China’s AI-related capex is conducted by the government. In the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), for instance, policymakers plan to invest RMB2tn in computing power networks, including data centers. China’s push for AI development and adoption is real, even though the way it is financed and applied differs significantly from the US. We now see Japan’s economy continuing to recover into H2 2026, as the negative impact of higher commodity prices is likely to be offset by the benefits of the ongoing AI boom, namely increased export volumes, higher export prices and the wealth effect. We expect the underlying inflation pressure to stay elevated as the AI boom and loose fiscal policy prop up aggregate demand, while cost pressure remains strong due to structurally higher oil prices and a weak yen. The stronger growth outlook reinforces our view that the Bank of Japan will raise interest rates faster than what the market currently expects. We anticipate the next hike in October, and see a risk of an earlier move, given the underlying fundamentals. records.text: 2 China Economics - AI Supercycle vs. Domestic Stagflation China's K-shaped economy appears to be playing out through the contrast between an AI supercycle and domestic stagflation. AI is driving industrial production and exports, with high-tech IP reaching a five-year high. But domestic demand is faltering, as retail sales contracted for the first time since Covid and FAI decline deepened. Steady CPI and broader PPI suggest stagflation risks are on the rise for the domestic economy. We maintain our headline GDP forecast at 4.5%YoY for 26Q2E and 4.7%YoY for 2026E. On policies, we see an acceleration of targeted support for domestic demand but not broad-based stimulus ahead. Investment- stabilization measures such as the “Six Networks” initiative are underway. Consumption and household income growth could be a key focus of July’s Politburo meeting. But an outright lift of budget deficit or government bond quota is not our base case, and monetary policy does not appear to be in the driver’s seat. records.text: Tech drives both the economy and the market The Chinese government is restructuring the economy by shrinking the property sector and bolstering the technology sector. This transformation is clearly reflected in physical output data. Compared with 2019 levels, production of industrial robots has tripled, and semiconductor production has more than doubled, in sharp contrast to the decline in construction materials such as glass and cement (Exhibit 5). The divergence is also visible in equity market performance. The Shanghai Composite Index has been largely flat year-to-date, but beneath the stable aggregate index, the information technology sector index has rallied by over 50%, while the consumer discretionary sector index has slid by more than 25% (Exhibit 6). Although policymakers have shown some concerns over the latest weakness in consumption growth, policy signals still point to unwavering support for tech and AI as China’s structural transformation continues. During its press conference after the May data release, for example, the NBS touted China’s technological advances in optical quantum computing and turbofan engine testing. According to NBS officials, high-tech manufacturing value-added grew 15.1% yoy, far outpacing overall IP growth of 4.5% yoy in May. The Truss episode was the clearest reminder that markets can shorten political timelines when fiscal credibility is questioned. Third, the electorate has become less forgiving. Real incomes have been squeezed, public services are under pressure, and housing affordability remains a generational fault line. That has weakened loyalty to both major parties and increased the threat from insurgent challengers. Leaders now operate in a permanent campaign environment, with local elections, by-elections and polling shocks quickly turning into leadership crises. The tolerance for mistakes (policy or personal) is very low. For financial markets, the lesson is not that every change of prime minister is automatically destabilising. The UK’s institutions remain deep, the Bank of England is independent, and policy continuity often survives personnel change. But the political risk premium has changed. Shorter premierships mean shorter policy horizons, less confidence in long-term reform and greater sensitivity around fiscal events. records.text: European Equity Strategy22 June 2026 ab 3 Within Europe, the divergence in positioning reflects differing starting points. Investors in core European countries, having generally remained defensively positioned, are now under-participating in the recovery, and face a more difficult decision on whether to rotate. By contrast, more opportunistic investors - particularly in northern Europe - have benefited substantially from more substantial investments in AI capex beneficiaries. One of the few areas of genuine consensus was banks. Across both European and global investors, the combination of strong capital returns, improved profitability and still- attractive valuations continues to anchor positioning. Few see an immediate catalyst to reduce exposure, even as the European business cycle seems to weaken and earnings revisions look to be peaking. Finally, there are early signs of idiosyncratic re-engagement within Europe from global stock-picking investors. Luxury, in particular, is attracting renewed interest, not on the basis of strong growth, but because the cycle of negative earnings revisions appears to be stabilising, while positioning is fairly light and valuations have cheapened substantially in recent years. We think this fits a broader pattern: investors are not yet ready to make large regional reallocations, but are increasingly willing to express more selective, bottom-up views. records.text: European June Flash PMI Preview The flash May PMIs surprised expectations to the downside, with the level of the composite Euro area index declining to 47.5, the lowest level in more than three years. In the final print, the composite index was revised up by a full point to 48.5, largely reflecting upward revisions to services activity. The last significant bond maturities are scheduled for June and July, with no further maturities thereafter, which will contribute to the heavy net bond supply (Figure 9). Although the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) has pledged to remain dynamic, we believe that this factor will cap and prevent huge selloffs but will not change the fundamental trend of a steeper curve in Thai rates. Similarly, BoT has also been increasing its holdings of ThaiGBs in the past few months, but this has not managed to reverse the steepening in Thai rates (Figure x).

Catalyst.Metric: South Africa 2026 local government elections; municipal vote shares; coalition dynamics

records.text: MK: Registered as a party for the first time in December 2023, MK won 14.6% nationally in 2024 and 45.9% in the province of KwaZulu-Natal. Its defining metro battleground in KZN is eThekwini, where it won about 48% of votes in 2024. Outside KZN, Gauteng provides spoiler capacity (MK took 13.2% in Johannesburg in 2024). MK’s main weakness in the 2026 LGE is that it has zero council governance track record. The party’s ward-level organisation is the key unknown. EFF: The Economic Freedom Fighters have weakened nationally, from a vote share of 10.8% in 2019 to 9.5% in 2024, as MK has cannibalised its anti-ANC base in KZN. It remains a kingmaker in the three metros in the province of Gauteng (12–14% in 2024). The EFF has indicated it will not align with GNU partners and prefers a tactical bloc with MK to deny either DA control or ANC confidence-and-supply (see MISTRA Barometer II). If the EFF and MK combine in Johannesburg and Ekurhuleni, a DA-led coalition would become arithmetically very difficult. Patriotic Alliance: The GNU-aligned PA (its leader Gayton McKenzie is a government minister) won 2.06% nationally in 2024 and is contesting all 257 municipalities this year versus 80 in 2021. The PA currently holds seats in four metros, and it has been peeling votes from the ANC and the DA in Coloured and working-class Black townships. In a Johannesburg by-election last October, for example, it won a ward from the ANC with 30% of the vote. SACP: After 30 years in alliance with the AN

records.text: 11 Municipal funding models differ: Overall, municipal government in South Africa receives less than 10% of revenues generated by the state, but this share belies significant differences among the 257 municipal entities across nine provinces. Understanding municipalities’ revenue reliance structure is key to extrapolating what’s at stake in the LGE 2026. The largest metro municipalities that run major cities are geared to generate more than 80% of their own revenues through electricity, water, refuse and sanitation charges as well as property rates and other taxes. In sharp contrast, rural municipal entities’ revenue streams rely heavily (>70%) on government grants, subsidies and donations. In between are numerous towns, large and small. Grave going concern issues in local government finances: The bulk of party campaigns centre around improving collapsed service delivery and fixing broken municipal finance models. The lower chart quantifies the share of municipalities in each province that face grave financial going-concern issues and/or are in breach of Municipal Finance Management Act obligations to sign off budgets with the requisite revenue streams already in place (i.e. they are approving unfunded budgets). Most municipalities’ finances continue to deteriorate due to to weak collection frameworks and rising bad debts – both households’ debt to municipalities and municipal debt governments’ ability to pay their own debts to service providers such as the state-owned energy

Hence, we prefer long USDILS in our model portfolio. records.text: vulnerable Portfolio inflows into US equities are dominated by two key regions: the Caribbean and the Euro Area. Within the EU, the largest inflow is not from the likes of Germany or France; rather, it is through Ireland, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg. In other words, US equity inflows are being driven by demand from financial centers. Its not clear which type of investor is operating through these regions, i.e. is it retail similar to Asia, fast money, or European real money rerouting for tax purposes. Regardless, this indicates that investors now are more actively managing their equity exposure in search of returns. Structurally, we think this makes the US financial account more vulnerable. If investors are now more actively rather than passively accumulating US equities, they will similarly be more willing to sell US equities if any signs of weakness were to emerge, which can actually translate into significant USD outflows. In other words, their holdings are now considerably less sticky than in the past. -30 -10 10 30 50 Feb-23 Oct-23 Jun-24 Feb-25 Oct-25 USD, billions Luxembourg Netherlands Germany France Ireland Net Euro Area

records.text: 2 Emerging Convictions Viewpoint | 22 June 2026 Warsh and peace Peace was a red herring. Investors positioned for a post-deal rally, but the Fed took away the punchbowl. We maintain the tactically cautious stance from our last Emerging Convictions - The stages of Iran grief: #3 (April 30). Global inflation remains high, and now the Fed is following other central banks in turning hawkish, while the rest of the world is seeing slower growth. At best, EM assets can hold up, but the risk is to the downside: any further jump in US data could lead to another DXY rally. We currently expect to stay cautious until the extent of Fed hikes has become clearer, and global growth has become more balanced again. However, towards year-end we should be able to look forward to a more favorable 2027 where global disinflation should favor EM fixed income. Echoes of the war Even after the Iran deal, the energy shock will cascade through the global economy. Rebuilding inventories to the pre-Iran levels will take two years according to our energy team, so energy inflation remains persistent until at least 1Q27 after which base effects should become favorable. At $80/bbl, Brent is still 10% higher YoY. Inflation is likely to continue to surprise to the upside as it typically does after oil spikes (Exhibit 1). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 alongside easing inflation could bring forward policy normalization in some jurisdictions, particularly where domestic demand remains resilient. Lower oil prices are also generally supportive across CEEMEA and Latin America through improved external balances and reduced inflation. In CEEMEA, the disinflationary impulse strengthens the case for earlier or deeper easing, while in Latin America the effects operate more indirectly via global financial conditions and Fed expectations. A combination of lower oil prices and a less hawkish Fed backdrop would create additional room for monetary easing, particularly in Mexico. Taken together, the evolving oil price outlook reframes the global policy debate. Rather than a single narrative dominated by inflation risks, central banks now face a more nuanced environment in which disinflation and growth resilience coexist. Over the next several weeks, the dominant question will be how durable the moves in oil prices prove, and how quickly policymakers adjust their frameworks in response.

records.text: M Update 2 May CPI Bank of Canada Implications The May CPI print is hotter at the headline level, but it is unlikely to materially change the Bank of Canada’s policy assessment. The Bank’s reaction function is not to respond mechanically to higher headline inflation, but to assess whether energy- driven price pressures are becoming generalized and persistent. Using this context, the May data still look contained. Headline inflation accelerated, and CPI excluding gasoline also firmed to 2.2%Y from 2.0%, but the non-gasoline pickup was concentrated in identifiable categories: airfares, travel tours, fresh produce, and computer equipment. None of these look like clean evidence of stronger domestic demand. Core inflation remains close to target. CPI-Trim was unchanged at 2.0%Y, CPI-Median was effectively unchanged at 2.1%Y, and all-items excluding food and energy rose 1.7%Y. The 3m annualized pace of ex-food-and-energy inflation rose but remains only 1.0%, while the preferred core measures are still broadly around target. That argues against a broadening in inflation pressure. Newsflow suggesting a resolution to the Strait of Hormuz crisis has driven energy prices materially lower. A lower energy path should also pull down the BoC’s near-term headline inflation projections, and mechanically, lowering its core inflation forecasts at the margin. Source: MiFiDII Post-trade Reporting Data, Barclays Research Converting transparency into actionable insights The introduction of a consolidated tape represents a step-change in data accessibility – but not necessarily in data quality. The tape aggregates existing post-trade transparency feeds without altering the underlying records. As such, issues such as duplicates or inconsistent flags remain embedded in the data. Any cleaning or deduplication must therefore be performed by data vendors or end users. A key challenge stems from cross-border reporting dynamics. In practice, this means that cross- border trades, such as between an EU-based client and a UK-based dealer, or vice versa, do not map cleanly to a single tape. Instead, they often appear in both UK and EU datasets, inflating volumes and introducing noise if not properly reconciled. This problem is exacerbated when trade flags are missing, misapplied, or inconsistent across jurisdictions. records.text: ry shock. Two and a half tests With the AI boom at full steam, the global economy will face two (and a half) important tests. The first one has to do with the stability of the energy matrix in the Middle East. The deal is temporary by design and fragile in nature. With normalization of energy flows priced to perfection, unexpected escalation coupled with tighter inventories can reaccelerate energy prices and disrupt supply chains. The second has to do with a sharper or more disorderly than expected tightening of global financial conditions, led by a more hawkish Fed amid a robust economy and persistent inflation dynamics despite lower energy prices. With accommodative fiscal and monetary policies helping absorb supply shocks and feed the AI-related investment boom, K-shaped consumption dynamics will be tested across many countries. The other (half a) test has to do with China and the tech boom in Asia. So far, the Chinese economy has shown strong resilience to the energy and trade shocks. But domestic demand remains fragile and the overall strategy continues to be exporting away its excess capacity. It remains to be seen how sustainable this is and how much the rest of the world can absorb it without triggering renewed geopolitical tensions. However, we noted clear unease about how much of that narrative is already priced, and the enthusiasm that appears to have developed in parts of the markets, such as the use of levered ETFs, call options and margin lending. Seemingly, these concerns are increasingly driving a reluctance to add incrementally, and a much greater focus on diversification. This is where the concept of market breadth has become central. This time is different (3): Pensions are overweight US assets We think the inflow into US equities in the 1990s had strong participation by longer term investor types than today. Pension funds for instance, were underweight US equities and so were actively increasing allocations. They are not doing so now. NBIM is one notable example. In 1998, 30% of their equity allocation was to the US while US stocks made up 53% of the global market cap. That equity exposure is now at 52%, 7% higher than their published benchmarks. So rather than increasing their exposure, this time around we see greater risks that they shift their allocation to be closer in line with the benchmark, suggesting space for active selling of USDs. Another example is in the Canadian pension system. The near-term pace remains elevated, with headline CPI running at 9.2% on a 3-month annualized basis, up from 7.5% in April. • Bank of Canada read-through: our view is that the BoC can look past the headline overshoot so long as core inflation stays contained and excess capacity in the economy persists. • The inflation impulse broadened somewhat beyond gasoline, with CPI excluding gasoline rising to 2.2%Y from 2.0%. However, the non-gasoline pickup was concentrated in a narrow set of categories—air transportation, travel tours, fresh fruit and vegetables, and computer equipment—rather than broad demand-sensitive inflation. • Core inflation remains contained. CPI-Trim was unchanged at 2.0%Y, while CPI-Median was effectively unchanged at 2.1%Y. All-items excluding food and energy rose only 1.7%Y, and its 3-month annualized pace remained close to 1.0%. • Gasoline is still doing most of the work. Gasoline prices rose 33.2%Y, contributing 1.3pp to headline CPI and adding roughly 19bp to the monthly change in headline contribution. Public transportation also added to the print, driven by air transport

SACP: After 30 years in alliance with the ANC, the South African Communist Party resolved in December 2024 to contest all wards independently. Shortly afterwards, the ANC national executive committee prohibited candidates from running for both parties. The SACP’s working-class metro base in parts of Ekurhuleni, Johannesburg and eThekwini could chip away some 2–4pp from the ANC in targeted wards, which could prove decisive in tight contests. Unite for Change (Rise Mzansi + BOSA + GOOD): Launched October 2025, Unite for Change is a single IEC-registered LGE entity combining three small GNU parties. It had a combined 2024 national vote share of under 1%, but with solid party leadership credentials. It has a metro focus on Johannesburg, Cape Town and eThekwini. It has declared it will not enter coalitions with the ANC, EFF or MK. ActionSA: The party declined to join Unite for Change, backing its own Gauteng brand. It is strongest in Johannesburg – where its leader, Herman Mashaba, was mayor in 2016–19 – and Tshwane. Its national vote share in 2024 was about 2%. The party’s natural alignment is with DA-led coalitions or a broad anti-ANC Gauteng bloc. records.text: t led by Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul's conservative Bhumjaithai Party secured a clear mandate, bringing an end to the recent turbulence. This marks a welcome conclusion to the political gridlock that had seen multiple prime ministers ousted over the past three years. We believe that the new government will prioritize economic growth by increasing spending, which is necessary for the country's development. The push for investments from the new government is already visible and should be supportive for growth. Tourism turning out better than expected: Despite initial concerns that the Middle East conflict this year would severely impact Thailand's tourism industry, the latest data suggests that tourist arrivals are holding up well. Currently, tourist arrivals are in line with last year's numbers and are consistent with pre-pandemic averages (Figure 4), which is a positive surprise. This resilience in tourism will be one of the factors contributing to the economy's stability in Q2. Notably, Chinese tourist arrivals have increased by 32% this year, rebounding from a lackluster performance last year. Business credit growth picking up: The demand for business investments is also reflected in credit growth. Since the start of this year, banks' credit growth for businesses has picked up, while consumer-side credit growth remains weak. This indicates that businesses are investing and expanding, which should have a positive impact on the economy.

records.text: 12 Emerging Convictions Viewpoint | 22 June 2026 Rates: pay the deal We think momentum over the summer is likely to favor paid positions as global inflation surprises are likely to remain on the upside. CTA positioning has been paid across the board for a while, but otherwise our sense is that positioning in payers is still moderate: most investors had wanted to avoid payers in the fear of a major rally on a possible Iran deal. However, now the deal is known, risks are skewed towards patchy implementation and still sticky energy prices, and the more hawkish Fed provides for another driver to push rates higher. Inflation risks becoming persistent Many investors have been arguing that the energy shock is transitory and should be looked through, but we’ve argued that this is true only in a minority of countries. Most of them have already been missing inflation targets before Iran, and even core inflation is above target in most countries—including the US. I nflation remains well anchored in only a few countries, including China (Exhibit 26). Need restrictive rates to be more bullish Given this elevated risk of inflation persistence in many markets, we would need rates to be restrictive, but we don’t think many markets meet this test. First off, the priced-in peak of the policy rate is above the 2027 forecast nominal GDP growth rate in only Brazil, Colombia, Mexico and South Africa (Exhibit 27). records.text: hould show in 2027. Fed hikes are now on the horizon The global economy will likely be tested by tighter financial conditions emanating from the US. The labor market firmed up and inflation dynamics have deteriorated in the US. While some one-offs are partly to blame, and tariffs should soon roll off, most of the FOMC seems to be losing patience after 5 years of high inflation. We have been clear that the economy was not asking for cuts and there is a lot of uncertainty on how the Fed will operate, but we now expect 75bp of Fed hikes this year, starting in September. Risks: Iran, financial conditions, K-shaped dynamics We have long pointed to stubborn inflation in the US triggering Fed hikes as a key risk to the outlook. In a context where loose financial conditions and AI have been driving stock markets and fueling K-shaped dynamics, the risk of a disorderly tightening of financial conditions may still be the Achilles’ heel of the global economy. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 25 June 2026 19 UK: BoE on hold in 2026, near-term risks still for a hike Sonali Punhani MLI (UK) Lower inflation and slightly better growth, BoE on prolonged pause Our expectation now of lower energy prices and less persistent energy shock implies less inflation and slightly better growth. We cut our inflation forecast to 3.1% (-20bps) in 2026 and to 2.3% (-10bps) in 2027. Inflation is still likely to rise in coming months but peak at a lower level of 3.3% in Sept/Nov. 2026 vs. 3.7% in Dec. before. We forecast 2028 inflation at 2.1%. Lower inflation shock can imply slightly better growth from H2 2026. At the same time, we no longer expect BoE hikes, which can help growth next year. We now expect growth at 1.1% (+10bps) in 2026 and 1.3% (+20bps) in 2027, still lower than pre-conflict levels. We forecast growth at 1.5% in 2028. We no longer have enough conviction to forecast hikes in our base case, but it remains a close call. We now expect the BoE to keep rates on hold in 2026 and deliver one 25bps cut in November 2027 to 3.5% (vs. our previous call of two hikes in 2026 and three cuts in 2027). We expect rates to be unchanged at 3.5% through 2028. Lower energy prices/less prolonged energy shock than we previously expected can lower risks of strong second round effects. This along with the BoE’s cautious approach, limited signs of domestic inflation rising and a still soft economy and labour market lead us to change our call to no hikes this year. T

records.text: Global Research estimates BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Price stability challenged by external shocks The impact of energy shock takes time to pass through In recent weeks, tensions between the US and Iran have shown signs of stabilization, and our global Commodities team now expects a moderation in global energy prices. Brent crude oil price is expected to fall to $79/b and $73/b in 3Q26 and 4Q26 respectively, averaging $82/b in 2026 before dropping further to $70/b in 2027. However, energy prices are still higher compared to a year-ago, and the impact of such global inflationary shock is set to passed through to the region with a lag. In April, headline inflation in EM Asia (on average) accelerated to close to 3%, up from 2.3% in March and 2.0% in February (Exhibit 37). The pass-through of the energy shock to domestic inflation remains mixed across the region, largely explained by differences in domestic fuel‑pricing mechanisms (see Asia Viewpoint: How fuel pricing shapes Asia’s inflation responses report), levels of energy import dependence, and the extent of fiscal support. Headline inflation spiked by 5% in the Philippines (where domestic fuel prices are largely market-driven) over the combined March–April period ( Exhibit 38), but rose by only around 0.5% in India, Malaysia, and North Asia (where domestic prices are largely controlled or adjusted). Since the onset of the war, particularly the energy sensitive CEE and Asia markets started to show much stronger correlations between their currencies and rates. This is intuitive as the energy price shock was both a balance of payments problem weakening the currencies and also an inflation problem pushing rates higher. However, for the rest of the EM (usually the more risk sensitive high beta complex), the correlations between FX and rates remain relatively similar to levels in developed markets. So, a normalisation in energy markets should once again bring down the correlations and help to sustain inflows in our view. Rates induced sell-off most risky for EM: In terms of total returns from local currency bonds in EM, this year the correlations with US equities and US rates has gone up significantly. Hence, a rates induced sell-off in risk assets could be the most damaging move for EM local bond portfolios. Silver lining: Despite the increased correlation of EM local bonds to Us rates and equities, EM FX carry still remained more secular. Especially EM high beta funded out of equity sensitive low yielding Asia mitigates some of the increased beta of the asset class.

records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 11 Other Regions Around the World In Canada, the BoC remained on hold at 2.25% in June, maintaining a wait-and-see approach amid a challenging macro backdrop. The key theme remains one of subdued growth, with higher trade costs, ongoing USMCA uncertainty and sharply slower population growth acting as persistent drags on consumption and labour markets. Growth is expected to remain below potential through 2026, with government spending continuing to provide the primary support to activity. While headline inflation is expected to temporarily approach 3% on higher energy prices, core inflation should remain contained below 2.2% through 2026-27 as excess supply, fading tariff pass-through and cooling shelter inflation offset external price pressures. We continue to expect the BoC to remain on hold through 2027, looking through the energy shock so long as core inflation and inflation expectations remain anchored. Risks remain two-sided, with persistent oil prices potentially requiring tighter policy, while a weaker global backdrop or adverse USMCA outcome could lower the bar for renewed easing. In Norway and Sweden, higher energy prices continue to create divergent growth and inflation dynamics. In Norway, Norges Bank paused in June after having delivered a 25bp hike in May, supported by elevated inflation and a resilient domestic economy. records.text: 34 Global Economic Viewpoint | 25 June 2026 Food inflation: a risk for early 2027 Food inflation is still moderate thanks to a good harvest in the 2025/26 farming season but could rise in early 2027. The near-term risk is higher fuel prices, as an input cost for farmers. Fertiliser prices remain elevated while supply is still fine. However, if supply problems were to come to the fore – such as an inability to deliver urea over the coming 2-3 months ahead of the planting season – prices could increase due to a supply shortage. That could mean lower output for the 2026/27 harvest and put pressure on food prices. We will also be closely watching the likely impact of the El Nino phenomenon on rains and agriculture output into early 2027. Nigeria: CBN on hold for longer The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) is still prioritising credibility. By keeping the policy rate at 26.5% in May, it is signalling that inflation risks still outweigh any near-term case for easing, even as the recent uptick remains relatively modest. We expect inflation to remain sub-20% by end-2026 before easing back toward 14% by end-2027, which is likely to keep the CBN on hold through the rest of this year. records.text: E M – L O CA L E YE S F O R A G L O B A L V IEW 323/06/2026 Japan, of course, has also been experiencing a significant negative terms-of-trade shock due to the Middle East crisis. Import prices for petroleum, coal and natural gas were up 34.9% y/y in May on a contract- currency basis. Even if the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens, we think a sustainable return of oil prices to pre-war levels is unlikely, given the structural supply loss and a likely sustained demand boost as inventories are drawn down. We assume that after a near-term dip, oil prices will climb to around USD85/bbl by year end (see Middle East: Barrel half full?, dated 17 June). That said, a well-performing global economy should make it easier for Japanese exporters to pass some portion of their higher energy costs through to their selling prices. We accordingly expect the negative impact of increased energy prices on the macro-level terms of trade to be offset to a meaningful degree by a rise in export prices driven by the AI boom. We note that exports of electric and electronic products totalled some JPY18.5trn for 2025, not very far from the JPY22.1trn figure for mineral fuel imports. Private consumption holding up well: As for the household sector, sentiment did take a sharp turn for the worse in March as the Middle East conflict escalated, but we have yet to see any evidence of spending being cut back. Lower headline inflation, but no easier monetary policy For inflation, lower energy prices should drive global inflation to a lower trajectory, though the bulk of our 30bp downward revision to global inflation is concentrated in developed markets, with more persistent inflation in the EM complex. For monetary policy, however, lower oil prices are unlikely to bring much relief. Beyond Fed hikes, we generally expect monetary policy to remain at least as tight, except in the UK. The big picture of global dynamics remains intact Behind our modest revisions is a global story that under the surface remains largely unchanged: the AI investment boom in the US and the K-shaped economy in the US, an overcapacity story in China, and a fragile European economy. AI investment and K-shaped dynamics in the US In the US, investment keeps having an outsized contribution to GDP growth even after growing at full speed and surprising to the upside last year (Exhibit 2). records.text: All About Tech An even more divergent economy China’s May activity data disappointed again following weak April readings. Both retail sales and fixed asset investment (FAI) contracted: May retail sales declined 0.6% yoy, and January-May FAI dropped 4.1% yoy. In the history of official releases, this is only the second time on record that both retail sales and FAI have printed negative numbers— the first was in 2020 during Covid lockdowns. Looking across major indicators, exports remain the best-performing sector, rising nearly 20% yoy in nominal USD terms. By contrast, domestic indicators such as property activity, auto sales, and infrastructure investment (on a single-month basis) showed double-digit year-over-year declines (Exhibit 1). Auto sales data best illustrate the significant divergence between exports and domestic demand: domestic sales dropped 22% yoy in May, while auto exports jumped 75% yoy (Exhibit 2). The April and May production data track roughly 4% yoy real GDP growth, about 1pp lower than the Q1 official real GDP growth of 5%. We calculate that the ongoing robust export growth likely contributes around 3pp to year-over-year real GDP growth, implying that domestic demand is growing at a very sluggish pace of only 1-2% yoy based on official statistics. This is also consistent with our import-implied domestic demand growth estimates. A Slower Q2 and a Faster Q3 Given the April and May realized data, we nudge down our Q2 real GDP growth forecast from 4.0% to 3.

Our base case is that the Fed will implement three rate hikes starting in December this year , and we also see an increasing risk of an earlier tightening (see June FOMC: Every meeting is live, dated 18 June). Against this backdrop, we expect the yen to remain under pressure. As the Bank of Japan repeatedly points out, companies have become more aggressive in their pricing strategies in recent years, which has accelerated both the degree and speed with which a weaker yen is passed on to consumer prices. Greater deployment of AI technologies may help to curb inflation through enhanced productivity over the medium to long term. But for the time being, we expect upward pressure on prices stemming from increased aggregate demand, yen weakness and structurally higher oil prices. But we think the tax cut should also add to upward pressure on underlying inflation as the resulting increase in consumers' purchasing power serves to boost aggregate demand.
