Consumption headwinds, but less severe than past cycles Downside risks to household consumption are building from the energy shock, higher interest rates, and rising inflation. However, the drag is likely to be less severe than in previous tightening episodes. In 2022, consumption slowed sharply to 0.1% before contracting in 3Q and remaining weak through 4Q, while in 2023 it declined in three of the four quarters amid an aggressive hiking cycle. By contrast, consumption recovered strongly from 2Q24 as the tightening cycle ended and rates began to ease. Given that the current cycle is expected to be relatively shallow – limited to around two hikes – the impact on consumption could be more moderate, pointing to a slowdown rather than a sustained contraction. Monetary policy outlook: one more hike Our policy rate outlook remains unchanged. We expect the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) to hike again in July following a first hike in May. Policy rate could peak at 7.25% and remain on hold for the rest of the year. Inflation is rising: 4% in April, likely peaking close to 5% by February 2027. We expect headline inflation to average 4.3% this year. Our baseline is contingent on the Iran deal holding up near term and the re-opening of Strait of Hormuz. Should the conflict re-escalate or continue into 2H26 with oil prices above US$100/bbl, we see risks of higher inflation and likely further rate hikes.

Gasoline still doing the heavy lifting: Transportation remains the dominant driver of the level and the monthly acceleration. The category contributed 1.7pp to headline CPI and added roughly 25bp to the monthly change in headline contribution. Within transportation, gasoline contributed 1.3pp to headline and added roughly 19bp on the month, with gasoline inflation rising to 33.2%Y from 28.6%. This remains a narrow energy shock rather than a generalized transportation cycle: purchase/leasing of passenger vehicles softened, while the pressure was concentrated in operation of passenger vehicles and gasoline. Airfares and travel services show cost pass-through, not broad services demand: Public transportation swung from a drag to a positive contributor, adding roughly 11bp to the monthly change in headline contribution. The move was concentrated in inter-city transportation, and specifically air transportation, where prices rose 7.4%Y after declining in April. Recreation also added to the print, with travel services contributing roughly 12bp, almost entirely through travel tours. records.text: ab 22 June 2026 Global Research Global Economic Perspectives Global growth nowcast - largest gap between hard/soft data since Liberation day Latest data suggests global growth slowed to 2.1% in May Our global nowcast suggests that median global growth momentum slowed from 2.9% in February, before the Middle East conflict, to around 2.1% in May. That is roughly one- third of a standard deviation below the post-1998 average of 2.85% (Figure 1). As a reminder, our nowcast tracks 370 monthly series across 28 countries, covering roughly 80% of global GDP . The dataset includes 270 hard indicators and 100 soft indicators. Almost all May soft data have now been released, but only around 25% of May hard data are available. We therefore fill the remaining observations using our in-house matrix-completion algorithm. The hard-soft gap is the widest since Liberation Day One notable feature of the current tracking is is the unusually large gap between hard and soft data momentum — the widest since Liberation Day (Figure 2). Surveys reacted quickly to the onset of the conflict in the Gulf, with implied global growth falling by roughly half (from around 3% to 1½%). Somewhat surprisingly, there was no reaction in the hard data; one reason for that we think is that the AI capex cycle is neutralizing a lot of the energy related disruption at the aggregate global level (see The Compendium). records.text: 30 Global Economic Viewpoint | 25 June 2026 Most central banks are in the hiking camp now Compared to our April forecast, we now expect more central banks to join the hiking camp over the rest of 2026 (Exhibit 41), as 1) growth acceleration become more visible in tech-centric economies, 2) impact of energy shock to kick in with a time lag, and 3) FX and capital outflow pressure deepened in several economies including Korea, Indonesia, Philippines and India. Within the hiking camp, we expect Bank Indonesia to tighten policy rates most aggressively, including a 25bp hike in 3Q following 100bp of tightening in 2Q26, to defend currency stability. We also expect one more 25bp hike from the RBI in 2026 (and one more in 1Q27) to prevent rapid INR depreciation amid a widening current account deficit. However, the real rate could become high next year if the Fed doesn’t cut. Thus, a key issue for EM in 2027 will become how determined the Fed is to return inflation to 2% quickly. records.text: Elections in a snapshot: South Africa's local government elections on 4 November 2026 will determine the composition of 257 municipal councils (4,488 wards), including eight metropolitan municipalities and 44 district municipalities. Just over 500 parties will compete for some 27.67 million registered voters (see Electoral Commission of South Africa). Local government receives about 8–9% of nationally raised revenue and constitutes the primary service-delivery interface for most citizens. Municipalities are responsible for the services, infrastructure and local governance systems that underpin economic activity and daily life. The eight metropolitan municipalities alone account for more than half of national economic output and almost half of all households. Ballot structure: Voters in the eight metros receive two ballots – proportional- representation party lists and ward candidates. In the 205 local municipalities, a third ballot is added for the district council PR vote. Seat allocation uses the ‘Droop quota’ (largest remainder) – the key structural driver of coalition proliferation, as it does not favour larger parties and lowers entry barriers for smaller ones. New rules for 2026 election: The Municipal Structures Amendment Act No. 3 of 2023 (LGMSAA) was passed in response to post-2021 dysfunction in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Nelson Mandela Bay. records.text: The past year: the roll-out of the new UK and EU bond transparency frameworks Both the UK and EU bond markets have been subject to post-trade transparency requirements since the introduction of MiFID II. However, in practice, this has not translated into effective transparency for two main reasons. First, data was fragmented across multiple venues, requiring market participants to source and aggregate it themselves, limiting usability. Second, prior to December 2025, extensive use of deferrals constrained the timeliness of the data. Regulatory timeline: from transparency reforms to data consolidation As shown in Figure 1, recent regulatory changes have improved the timeliness of the data. The UK introduced its new transparency regime in December 2025, followed by the EU in March 2026. These changes have led to a clear increase in real-time reporting, with the majority of trades (by count) now reported on a near-immediate basis. The next milestone is the consolidation of all this data. This process is already underway in the UK with the launch of the consolidated tape on 22 June 2026, operated by Etrading Software (ETS), which aggregates all UK-executed trades into a single source. A similar tape is expected in the EU by late 2026 or early 2027, operated by Ediphy, bringing together trades executed across EU markets. FIGURE 1. The TIC data are released with a six-week lag, but higher-frequency data give us a read on developments since, albeit for a smaller swath of the investor base. We will have to see if markets challenge the Fed's current stance on the RMP or the Treasury's current level of buybacks. Bottom line, we believe last week's Fed meeting set the stage for a new regime under which the Fed may be willing to take some short term pain in markets to establish a higher chance of success in its longer term goals to support the administration's "Run it Hot" / rebalancing strategy. We commend this approach but wonder how it will react if markets test its resolve. It's possible such a test may be forthcoming over the next few weeks as the rate of change on liquidity interacts with the rate of change peak in earnings revisions as discussed in last week's note. Although an extension remains plausible, our baseline is that no extension will be agreed on July 1 (see report). Without an extension, USMCA would remain in force but shift to annual reviews and would expire in 2036 unless extended. Tariffs on autos, steel, and aluminum are also likely to remain in place, keeping trade uncertainty elevated and weighing on investment. records.text: jections. Softer gasoline prices would lower headline CPI directly and, mechanically, should also weigh modestly on core measures through fuel-sensitive services. While the May CPI print was hot, the upside remained concentrated in identifiable relative-price shocks rather than broad domestic demand, supporting our view that the BoC can remain on hold. Fresh produce lifted grocery inflation: Food inflation firmed to 3.8%Y, with food purchased from stores rising to 4.3%Y. The grocery impulse was concentrated in fresh produce. Fresh fruit rose 5.3%Y and added about 5bp to the monthly contribution change, while fresh vegetables rose 9.0%Y and added about 4bp. That was partly offset by softer meat, bakery products, and other food products. The composition points to supply and fuel-cost pressure rather than stronger household demand. AI/chips are visible, but too small to change the macro story: Computer-related prices are beginning to show some upward pressure, consistent with higher prices for RAM and SSDs amid AI-related data-centre demand and limited production capacity. Digital computing equipment and devices moved back into positive inflation territory and added a little over 1bp to the monthly contribution change. We expect this pressure to persist, but the basket weight of under 1% is too small to materially alter the aggregate core inflation outlook. In Chipflation – Navigating A Memory Crisis, we discuss these dynamics in detail.

records.text: Marija Veitmane 25 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Time to give Software another look? Software has been one of the market’s biggest casualties, hit by AI disruption fears and collapsing positioning. But with fundamentals stabilizing and investors rotating back in, the setup is looking more like an opportunity than a risk. Software is one of the worst-performing industry groups in the US, losing over a third of its value over the past twelve months (only Real Estate and Commercial Services fared worse). This underperformance is particularly striking given the strength elsewhere in IT. As the earnings outlook deteriorated—amid fears that AI would cannibalize software revenues— investors fled, cutting holdings to record lows (Figure 1). On the fundamentals, earnings have declined for two consecutive quarters, driven primarily by weaker sales while margins held up (Figure 2). This suggested some client hesitation to renew or sign new contracts, potentially substituting toward AI tools. However, commentary from the latest reporting season has been more reassuring. Management at larger software firms emphasized the stickiness of their offerings —particularly in cyber security, data protection, and proprietary datasets—making them difficult to displace, especially for corporates. Routing trades towards UK venues The market consensus is that the UK transparency framework is both simpler and better calibrated compared to the EU, particularly in how it treats larger trades through longer deferrals. For example, a €10mn trade in a liquid investment-grade corporate bond would be reported with a two-week delay in the UK. In the EU, by contrast, the same trade would be reported much more quickly: while volume may still be deferred, the price is typically published within one day. In many cases, we think that the availability of the price alone is sufficient for the market to infer the likely size of the trade. A similar pattern holds in sovereigns: a €50mn trade in a liquid government bond would be reported after two weeks in the UK, whereas in the EU the price would again be visible within a day. Anecdotally, some clients expect this difference in calibration to lead to a gradual shift in activity towards UK venues. records.text: US firms can produce competitive goods for a lower cost than foreign counterparts, there is a larger profit for the American company. This translates into upward pressure on wages, which firms in the non- tradeable sector must match. To offset that increase in wages without the accompanying productivity boost, these non-tradeable firms must then raise prices, in turn boosting the overall price level. When accompanied by higher yields, this then strengthens the currency. Higher productivity in non-tradeable sector can weigh on FX However, the opposite happens if the productivity boost occurs in the non-tradeable sector. Domestic firms drive competition, meaning that with a productivity boom they may reduce prices to attract more customers, in turn dampening inflationary pressures, contributing to declining yields and thus a weaker currency. In this instance, higher productivity would actually be FX- negative. AI to disproportionately improve non-tradeable sector productivity Our expectation is that AI will disproportionately boost productivity in non-tradeable sectors, i.e. services. That’s not to say that tradeable sectors will see no benefit. After all, the US is already a large producer of high-value exports. However, more fragmented global trade policy and tariffs may play a role in diminishing that effect. Data tends to support this. records.text: Japanese investors were substantial net buyers in the first half of May, but turned to modest net selling at the end of the month. In foreign equities and funds, Japanese investors accelerated their net selling to JPY2.7trn as overseas equity markets moved higher. By investor type, trust accounts logged their largest sales (JPY3.4trn) under comparable data since 2005, suggesting a rebalancing from equities into bonds. By contrast, investment trusts, presumably driven by the New NISA program for retail investors, continued to record net purchases (JPY0.6trn). Weekly data show that investment in foreign equities continued to trend mostly in net selling territory through May, except during the middle of the month. In the other direction1 , foreigner investment in Japanese securities remained firm against the backdrop of higher yen rates and stronger equities. In equities, net purchases slowed to JPY2.9trn from a record JPY9.4trn in April, but still showed a rapid pace of buying. Net purchases of medium/long-term bonds also remained solid at JPY0.9trn, close to the previous month’s JPY1.0trn. Meanwhile, net selling of bills moderated further to JPY0.7trn. Weekly data show that inward investment in Japanese equities turned to net selling at the end of May for the first time in two months, while inward investment in Japanese bonds accelerated in the latter half of May. 22 June 2026 3 Barclays | JPY Flows Monthly - May 2026

Given the more benign inflation profile, we move forward our call for quarterly cuts to March- 27 (from June-27), but we expect the ECB to pause at 2% depo again. The persistent inflation undershoot in 2028 will ultimately force their hand into cuts to 1.5% one year later. It is our old scenario (pre-war), delayed from the energy shock. Why is a “one and done” not done? A simple way to argue that a September hold is not a done deal is to compare energy prices today with different ECB scenarios. But before that, remember what we have been arguing for a while. First, the ECB baseline scenario in June was consistent with 50bp of total hikes, with risks of 25bp more. Even the mild scenario was consistent with 50bp, with a marginal risk of a bit less. Meanwhile, back in March, as flagged by ECB President Lagarde several times, the baseline scenario was consistent with two hikes. Market pricing of oil today is certainly below the ECB’s baseline from June, and that creates downside to inflation forecasts. But it’s still above the ECB’s mild scenario in June and not far from their baseline in March. For gas the picture is similar, with prices close to the March baseline (Exhibit 21). We applaud this move as a means to keep the market on its toes while providing the Fed a greater ability to have shock value, when necessary, in pursuit of its goals. As the same time, Warsh also indicated he is more focused on the left side of the decimal place when considering inflation. That suggests he might be ok with inflation between 2-3 percent rather than a hard target of 2 percent. While subtle, we think it indicates the Chair is fully aware of the need to run the economy hot to some extent if they have a real chance of managing the debt problem in the long term. In other words, this is going to be a balancing act of letting the economy boom (higher real and nominal GDP growth) while not losing control of the bond market, particularly the back end (both rate levels and volatility). As usual, we take our cues from the markets in how we interpret this new messaging. This means that the central banks which mostly reacted to higher oil prices are being let off the hook. As per Figure 15, those are central banks in the UK, Sweden and the EU, where front ends have been most sensitive to oil prices. Second, the June FOMC was a hawkish surprise, suggesting that chair Warsh may not be as likely to bat back against his hawkish colleagues on the committee as envisioned. While falling oil prices will also help the Fed, the US is the only large country benefiting from the growth impulse from the AI boom, and it can therefore be argued that the risk is that even with a fading oil shock, rates will eventually have to rise, even though we note that this is not the base case of Citi’s US economics. records.text: Jan Hatzius +1(212)902-0394 | jan.hatzius@gs.com Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC Global Views: More Crude, Less Concern 22 June 2026 | 6:10AM EDT 1. The agreement between the US and Iran has reduced the downside risks to our economic outlook. Our commodities strategists now see Brent crude at $80 per barrel by the end of 2026, with two-sided risks. On the upside, Iran’s announcement on Saturday that the Strait was closed again served as a reminder that oil flows might only recover slowly. On the downside, a near-term glut could develop as oil is released quickly into a market that was already oversupplied before the war. The agreement has led us to cut our 12-month US recession risk estimate further from 25% to the long-term norm of 15%. (This is below our 20% estimate on the eve of the war because the labor market improvement since then indicates greater underlying resilience.) 2. Alongside the cut to our recession risk estimate, we have nudged up our sequential H2 GDP growth forecast to 2%. The slightly stronger path reflects a positive sequential impulse to real income from lower gas prices, at a time when the economy continues to benefit from the AI boom via higher equity wealth as well as strong capex. But we still expect growth to remain moderate. First, AI capex largely consists of goods that are imported from Asia and, in the case of semiconductors, don’t even show up in GDP . Second, even with the drop in gas prices, real income defined on a cash flow basis is likely to slow

But is a productivity boost always FX positive? Not necessarily. We think it is important to draw a distinction between whether the productivity boom is in firms producing tradeable vs nontradeable goods. Boost in productivity for the tradeable goods sector is FX positive According to the Balassa Samuelson theory, an increase in productivity in the tradeable goods sector is FX positive. This is because costs of goods are determined by global demand, and if US firms are able to produce competitive goods for a lower cost relative to non - US counterparts, then there is a larger profit for the US company. This translates into upwards pressure on wages, which firms producing non - tradeable must match. To offset that increase without the accompanying productivity boost, these non - tradeable firms must then raise prices, which boosts the overall price level. When accompanied by higher yields this then strengthens the currency. Boost in productivity for the non - tradeable goods sector can weigh on FX These firms tend to keep wages steady, but if there were to be any broad - based move to raise wages it would likely prove negative for the tradeable sector. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 25 June 2026 27 Growth divergence across AI-beneficiaries vs others As a result, exposure to global AI demand, especially that from the US, will be a key determinant of growth outlooks in 2026 and 2027. Taiwan and Korea are at the core of this cycle due to their leadership in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, while several ASEAN exporters also benefit from their integration into the supply chain. By contrast, growth in economies with limited exposure to AI is driven more by domestic demand, which is also more exposed to shock from higher energy prices. Robust growth driven by exports in Taiwan & Korea Taiwan and Korea, with direct exposure to the AI and semiconductor cycle, have delivered strong export performance year-to-date, and above-trend growth momentum is likely to continue through 2027. Export momentum has been strongest in Taiwan, where headline exports grew 46% year-on-year year-to-date, driven by strong shipments of tech components for cloud and high-performance computing. Not far behind, Korea’s exports rose 41% year-on-year year-to-date, led by advanced semiconductors and supported by higher DRAM prices and a spike in hard disk exports. As a result, we expect net exports to contribute around half of headline GDP growth in both economies. The surge in external demand is also spilling over into domestic demand. The surplus is helping to build international reserves, which represent a chronic problem in Ecuador, and dissipate concerns about the balance of payments. Meanwhile, economic activity is showing a healthy pace, more domestic demand-driven (and presumably labor- intensive) than last year. Increasing business confidence and fast-growing credit to firms, suggests a stronger expansion of private investment. The main risk is electricity blackouts triggered by El Niño Arguably, one of the main vulnerabilities of the Ecuadorean economy is the fragile equilibrium between electricity supply and demand. Supply is not catching up with demand, which means even a modest shock to the system can cause blackouts (that exact a heavy cost on economic activity). In 2023, blackouts happened because drought conditions affected the functioning of hydroelectric generators (the bulk of the system). In 2026 there is a growing risk of a global El Niño climate shock (aka zone 3/4) that in Latin America is typically associated with droughts. In Ecuador, the dry season – when El Niño may hit the hardest – begins in September/October. We forecast GDP growth of 3.2% for 2026, 2.7% for 2027, and 3% for 2028. records.text: pronouncements indicate no interest in a successor IMF program in 2027. Authorities indicate continued GCC Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) on commercial terms. Assuming the global backdrop is supportive, enabling Emerging Markets (EM) carry trades with continued GCC FDI and high domestic real rates, Egypt will likely be in a position to bridge its external funding needs without another IMF program in 2027. The policy mix post-IMF in 2027 bears watching. Technocrats could hold the line on maintaining the primary surplus at 5% of GDP for now and real rates could remain elevated. However, the near-term flexibility of the Egyptian Pound (EGP) may not remain materially so post-IMF, raising medium-term risks to competitiveness. CIS: capitalizing on (geo)politics and reforms The macro case of the broader Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) region has reaped material benefits from the latest geopolitical tensions given its energy/food independence as well as its limited logistical exposure to Gulf. The main energy exporters (Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan) strongly benefitted from the run-up in energy costs, as some countries (Georgia, Armenia and, to some extent, Uzbekistan) managed to capture new tourism flows diverted from the Gulf. The oil price spike had a relatively lower impact on regional inflation given the lack of supply disruptions and bilateral energy pricing but still delayed the previously expected start of easing cycles in Uzbekistan and Ukraine.

We believe the NBH’s policy rate will reach 5.25% by year end (with some downside risks following the June meeting), and the board can continue to cut next year to reach low 4% handles. We anticipate a wait-and-see approach from the Czech National Bank following its pre-emptive hike in June and a hold at 3.75% during our forecast horizon. Recent data weakness in Poland has prompted some National Bank of Poland board members to hint at the possibility of more cuts, but we think this is premature as we only see inflation heading back towards the target in the second half of 2027. We see the South African Reserve Bank as the most pre- emptive CEEMEA central bank. We expect the SARB to deliver another 25bp hike in the July meeting, despite the moderation in energy prices. A hawkish monetary-policy stance can support the convergence of inflation back towards the SARB’s 3% target next year, and we still see room for cuts next year with very elevated ex-ante real rates (see South Africa: Proactive SARB to flatten front- end rates, dated 5 May). The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, on the other hand, is likely to normalise its open market operations back to weekly repo auctions at 37% in Q3, in our view, and should deliver some gradual cuts in Q4 to finish the year at 35%. We expect the BSP to deliver a further 75bp of tightening, reaching 5.5% by 4Q26. Across the CEEMEA region, against an uncertain energy outlook, we see growth softening rather than stalling. Persistent inflation risks make future easing cycles conditional on expectations and underlying core measures. Some central banks may temporarily reverse course. In Turkey, the CBT is expected to keep the policy rate unchanged at 37% in the near term as disinflation has stalled. CPI is expected to average 31.6%Y in 2026, while GDP growth is forecast at 2.5% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027. As energy prices ease in 2H26, we expect the CBT to restart its easing cycle, cutting by 200bp in 4Q26 and taking the policy rate to 35% by year-end. Further gradual easing should follow in 2027, with the policy rate reaching 27.50% by year-end, though risks remain skewed toward tighter policy if energy prices or global rates rise further. In Egypt, the CBE is expected to remain on hold through 2026 as inflation remains volatile and external risks persist. GDP growth is forecast at 4.8% in 2026 and 5.0% in 2027, while average inflation is expected at 13.3%Y in 2026. records.text: sector shifted back into net buying. Private investors bought $80bn of long-term US fixed income in April, down from $114bn in March. Meanwhile, the official sector bought $18bn, after having been sellers the prior two months. At the same time, foreign investors reduced T-bills by $14bn in April, extending the $17bn decline in March that followed unusually strong buying of $92bn in February. The April decline was driven by private-sector reduction, while the official sector remained a net buyer, adding $16bn. Across products, demand broadened and rotated away from the credit-heavy pattern seen in March and back into Treasuries and agencies: • Treasuries demand strengthened notably. Net purchases of long-term USTs rose to $51bn in April, a sharp increase from $14bn in March and well above the average pace of $20-30bn per month. Both private and official investors contributed: private demand of $34bn was broadly in line with the 12-month average, while official investors added $16bn, marking a notable turnaround from the prior two months. • Agencies demand also rebounded. Foreign investors bought $27bn of agencies in April, compared with $4bn of net selling in March. The pickup was entirely driven by private investors ($28bn), while official demand was slightly negative (-$1bn). Europe bought $61bn in April, up from $35bn in March and well above recent averages, with about half of the net inflows directed toward long-term Treasuries. Demand continued to be led by financial centers: The UK bought $45bn in total, including $26bn in long-term Treasuries, while Luxembourg added $13bn also primarily in Treasuries and agencies, though each reduced $9bn in T-bills. Belgium was a notable seller, offloading $12bn in USTs, but this likely reflected some custodial activities. Meanwhile, Spain also reversed course, buying $12bn in long-term USTs in April after selling similar amount in March, while Germany sold $5bn following $10bn of purchases in the prior month. Asia shifted back into net buying, with $55bn of inflows after two months of selling but broadly matching the pace seen in January. BoE on hold in 2026, near-term risks still for a hike We no longer have enough conviction to forecast hikes in our base case, but it remains a close call. We now expect the BoE to keep rates on hold in 2026 and deliver one 25bps cut in November 2027 to 3.5% (vs. our previous call of two hikes in 2026 and three cuts in 2027). We expect rates to be unchanged at 3.5% through 2028. Lower energy prices/less prolonged energy shock than we previously expected can lower risks of strong second round effects. This along with the BoE’s cautious approach, limited signs of domestic inflation rising and a still soft economy and labour market lead us to change our call to no hikes this year. The balance of risks still leans towards a hike this year on re-escalation risks or strong second round effects emerging. Next year, we expect a cut in November 2027 to 3.5%. The cut to our terminal of 3.5% won’t be easy. Fiscal and political outlook Political uncertainty and leadership change have increased near term policy uncertainty, which could weigh on growth. records.text: eads to outflows from EM assets. This time around, we expect USD strength to be less pronounced, and, despite the Fed outlook, our revised FX forecasts imply a flat USD TWI through year-end. Diversification of global portfolios away from the USD— and the resulting structural flows—should partially offset the cyclical tailwind the greenback receives from higher rates and limit the impact on EM. We also think 75bp of tightening would leave the Fed’s policy stance short of being excessively restrictive, especially given the starting point of elevated inflation, robust earnings growth, loose fiscal policy and tight labour markets. Consequently, these hikes seem unlikely to derail the global risk backdrop (and EM carry) completely, even if the rate path could be bumpier with bouts of volatility (Figure 1). We therefore see EM local-currency bond returns remaining moderately positive for the rest of the year. We expect a total return of around 3.2 % from the asset class, using our new FX and rates forecasts. This is still in positive territory, but it is much lower than our 8.1 % forecast at the start of the year and the 20 % total return that EM local-currency bond portfolios delivered last year. As a result, we have revised our model portfolio for EM local bonds to reflect a view that focuses more on idiosyncratic views and relative value trades.

Baseline estimate: 5% drawdown to EURUSD For EURUSD, the model fair value estimate declines 5% through to 2034 (Figure 1). This reflects US productivity growth surpassing that of the eurozone. We would note here that the impact on our model is primarily productivity-driven. A widening of the US output gap relative to the eurozone has minor impact on our projections given the model’s small coefficient. Further, our economists do not foresee the rate differentials widening to a degree that would suffice to drive a material change in fair value. But is a productivity boost always FX-positive? Not necessarily. We think it is important to distinguish between a productivity boom affecting firms in the tradeable versus non-tradeable sectors. Better productivity in tradeable goods is FX-positive According to the Balassa Samuelson theory, increased productivity in the tradeable goods sector is FX-positive. This is because costs of goods are determined by global demand, and if US firms can produce competitive goods for a lower cost than foreign counterparts, there is a larger profit for the American company. Diversification of global portfolios away from the USD – and the resulting structural flows – should partially offset the cyclical tailwind the greenback receives from higher rates, and limit the impact on EM. We think 75bp of tightening would leave Fed policy short of being excessively restrictive, especially given the starting point of elevated inflation, robust earnings growth, loose fiscal policy and tight labour markets. These hikes would therefore be unlikely to entirely derail the global risk backdrop (and EM carry), even if the rate path could be bumpier with bouts of volatility (Figure 1). Recent data show that around 70% of its total exports fall under the USMCA exemption (Figure 4), while several key sectors-and roughly 3 million jobs -are linked to the agreement. US rhetoric toward Canada has turned more hawkish, with the US Trade Representative arguing that Canada must make unilateral concessions and describing the unresolved issues as “significant.” The main pressure point s are autos and rules of origin. Canada’s supply chains are deeply integrated, with components often crossing the border several times before final assembly. The US is now seeking tougher domestic - content requirements, including a 50% US -made threshold; under current rules, there is no US -specific minimum. Such a shift could disrupt supply chains and lower Canadian GDP by 2 –3%. Dairy is smaller in economic terms but is also politically sensitive, particularly in Quebec and Ontario, where the sector is concentrate d in important electoral regions. Canada wants to preserve supply management, while the US is pushing for greater market access, making this a difficult issue to resolve. If the US secures broader access, Canadian GDP could fall by as much as 0.5%. Canada is already showing signs of strain ahead of the USMCA review. Growth forecast unchanged, but rebalancing downgraded We maintain our GDP growth forecasts at 4.5% for both 2026 and 2027 and extend our projection to 2028 at 4.3% (Exhibit 15). However, we lower our expectations for rebalancing, reflecting stronger exports and weaker domestic demand. We now forecast retail sales growth at 1.8% yoy this year, given limited prospects for additional policy support to consumption. While housing activity has improved in some major cities, a nationwide stabilization is still needed to drive a sustained recovery in consumer demand. FAI growth is expected to remain positive, at around 2.0%, supported by improving PPI inflation, the ongoing “six-network” infrastructure construction, and a lower year-ago base in the second half. However, infrastructure spending is likely to act more as a buffer against weakness elsewhere rather than a significant driver of growth (see report: ‘Six networks' to drive an investment upturn ). By contrast, we upgrade our export growth forecast to 15.0% in 2026, supported by AI- related capex, rising global demand for renewable energy equipment and EVs, and higher prices.
